newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. Mideast peace drive runs out of steam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Mideast peace drive runs out of steam.

text.p: U.S. Middle East peace efforts received another setback on Thursday when Palestinians rejected an American compromise date for an Israeli troop withdrawal in the West Bank.

Western sources said Washington envoy Dennis Ross could return home on Friday if separate meetings with Palestinian officials and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanayahu late on Thursday failed to break the redeployment timetable deadlock.

Ross has been shuttling for weeks between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to pin down an elusive deal on an Israeli withdrawal in Hebron. But Arafat, suspicious of Netanyahu's commitment to wider Palestinian self-rule, has been holding out for guaranteed dates for further pullbacks in the rest of the West Bank.

"Israel has proposed to end the last stage of further redeployments from the rest of the West Bank in 1999. We rejected that," said Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, general secretary of the Palestinian presidency. "So to break the deadlock in the talks Ross proposed as a compromise mid-1998, and we rejected this as well," he told Reuters.

"The Palestinian leadership will not make and cannot make any more compromises, especially on dates stated in the original agreement and the U.S. compromise is a violation of the deal that was signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton," Abdel-Rahim told Reuters. "
Western diplomats said talks on extending Palestinian self-rule appeared bogged down.
"Both sides are now playing the blame game. There's not much more Ross can do for the moment," said one diplomat.

Both Netanyahu and Arafat accuse each other of delaying the talks. Negotiators say a deal on Hebron is all but reached. The argument now is over the timing and scope of three further redeployments which should be completed by September 7 this year under the Oslo peace accords.

Netanyahu, facing a revolt by as many as seven of his 18 cabinet ministers if he hands back Hebron, wants to extend redeployment into 1999, partly to strengthen his hand in talks on a final settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Arafat wants to be in control of the 90 percent of the West Bank he believes should be his under Oslo before negotiating such sensitive "final status" issues as Jerusalem, refugees and the powers of a Palestinian government.

"We are going to continue talks," said PLO official Mahmoud Abbas before meeting Ross on Thursday. "They should have a response on the dates. If we succeed on agreeing on fixed dates for further redeployments we could be moving ahead," he told Reuters.
Israeli and U.S. officials were tight-lipped in public. Privately a U.S. official said Ross would decide after meeting Netanyahu whether it was worth staying in the region.
Arafat was also waiting for the outcome of Ross's meetings to determine whether he should leave for a scheduled European trip on Friday, PLO officials said.
